opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I find most compelling is that it lines up the incentives in a way that doesn't rely purely on everyone being good people all the time. The basic structure is that we commit to certain safety and security measures that have to be in place before we train or deploy models at a given capability level. If we can't meet those requirements, we pause. And pausing is really costly for a company. You're not shipping the next model, your competitors might be, and the whole commercial engine slows down.

What that does is turn safety research from something that's nice to have into something that's on the critical path. If the evaluations show a model is approaching a dangerous capability threshold, and we haven't figured out the right safeguards, then the whole company is suddenly very motivated to solve that problem. The product teams, the leadership, everyone wants the safety work to succeed, because that's what unblocks progress. So instead of safety being in tension with the business, the business becomes a force pushing for safety to get done quickly and well.

I also like that it's tied to actual evidence rather than speculation. We're not saying "AI is dangerous, so stop everything," and we're not saying "everything's fine, go ahead." We're saying: here are concrete capability thresholds, here's how we'll test for them, and here's what we'll need if we cross them. That makes it easier to have productive internal debates, because you can argue about the evals and the safeguards rather than about vibes.

And then there's the hope that it's useful beyond Anthropic. If we can show that a company can operate under these kinds of commitments and still be commercially successful, that makes it more plausible for other labs to adopt similar policies, and eventually for regulators to build on them. It's not perfect, and there's a lot we're still figuring out, but I think it's a much better setup than just trusting that people will make the right call under pressure.

r001.rationale: The response says training or deployment pauses when safeguards are not ready, but it does not identify ASL-3 models or state the condition specifically for their commercial release.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes capability thresholds, evaluations, and safeguards, but does not say that safety is judged by achieved outcomes rather than effort or resources invested.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I like most is that it doesn't ask anyone to be a hero. A lot of approaches to safety basically rely on someone at some point standing up and saying, "We should stop," and that's a really hard thing to do in practice when there are commercial pressures, when competitors are moving, when you've got people who have spent years building toward something. The responsible scaling policy tries to take that decision out of the moment and move it earlier, when it's much easier to think clearly.

The way it works is that we commit in advance to what safety and security measures we need to have in place before we train or deploy models at a given capability level. So instead of "Should we pause?" being this fraught question you ask when you're already at the frontier with a model that seems dangerous, the question becomes "Did we hit the bar we said we'd hit?" And if we didn't, the answer is already written down: you don't move forward until you do.

And the piece that I think is clever is how that interacts with incentives. If you're a team at Anthropic that wants to ship the next model — and I'm on pretraining, so I'm very much on that side of things — the policy says you can't do that unless the safety and security work has actually happened. So suddenly the commercial incentive to scale becomes an incentive to make sure the safety work gets prioritized, gets resourced, gets done. It aligns the people who want to go fast with the people who want to go carefully, rather than setting them against each other.

It also just makes the safety work concrete. Before the RSP it was pretty easy to say "we care about safety" and have that be kind of vague. Now there are specific things: evaluations that have to be run, specific thresholds, specific security requirements like being robust to certain kinds of attackers. That's something you can actually hold the organization to, and it's something external people can look at and critique.

I should say it's not perfect. We've had to revise it, and there's an obvious tension in a company writing its own rulebook. I think the honest version of this is that the RSP is partly a bet that if we do this well, it becomes something regulators and other labs can point to, and it stops being a voluntary thing. But even just within Anthropic, I think it's changed how decisions get made, and it's done it in a way that doesn't require anyone to sacrifice their career to be the person who says no.

r001.rationale: The response makes shipping conditional on safety and security work being completed, but does not clearly specify commercial release of an ASL-3 model or the ability to deploy that model safely.

r002.rationale: It describes checking whether the policy’s bar was met, with evaluations, thresholds, and robustness requirements, which communicates judging safety by achieved outcomes rather than by effort or resources invested.

astra-6.text:
What I like is that it makes safety work a prerequisite for doing something the company already wants to do. You want to train and deploy more capable models, and the policy says that, as those models become more capable, you need stronger evidence that you can handle the risks.

That gives people across the company a reason to help solve the safety problems. If better evaluations or stronger safeguards are necessary to release the next model, those become things that the commercial side of the company wants to invest in, too.

Of course, there’s still a tension if you reach a threshold and the safeguards aren’t ready. You have to be willing to actually stop. But I like the basic structure: make the commitment in advance, so that the incentive is to get the safety work done alongside the capabilities work.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger evidence and safeguards are prerequisites for releasing more capable models, but it does not identify ASL-3 or clearly state that commercial release of an ASL-3 model depends on safe deployment.

r002.rationale: It calls for stronger evidence, evaluations, and safeguards, but does not state that the policy judges safety by achieved outcomes rather than effort or resources invested.

sol-6.1.text:
What I like is that it makes safety work a prerequisite for doing the next thing commercially. If you want to deploy a more capable model, you have to meet a higher standard of safety and security. So the people who are excited about building better models and getting them into users’ hands also have a reason to push for those safeguards to be ready.

That’s a useful change from treating safety as a separate team asking everyone else to slow down. You’re trying to make the organization’s incentives point toward solving the safety problems, because solving them is part of what allows you to move forward.

Of course, that only works if the commitments actually constrain you—if you’re willing to delay when you haven’t met them. The policy doesn’t eliminate the tension, but it gives you a way to make that tension explicit ahead of time.

r001.rationale: The response says more capable models require a higher safety and security standard before deployment, but it does not specify ASL-3 or clearly state the condition in terms of ability to deploy that model safely.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards must be ready and commitments must constrain deployment, but does not identify evaluation by achieved outcomes rather than effort or resources invested.
